system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 19 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2145-08-14 10:56:00 to 2145-09-01 13:40:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with fever, left flank pain, and purulent drainage from his left nephrostomy tube, consistent with a genitourinary tract infection. He had recently completed treatment for a right foot cellulitis. Admission labs showed leukocytosis and elevated creatinine. Imaging revealed decompression of the renal collecting systems without abscess. Cultures from the nephrostomy tube and urine grew Group A Streptococcus and E. coli, guiding antibiotic therapy. Blood cultures showed coagulase-negative staph, likely a contaminant. He was started on meropenem and later transitioned to ertapenem via a PICC line for a two-week course. His infection resolved with normalization of vital signs and labs. A 5 mm left lung nodule was incidentally found on CT, requiring follow-up. He was discharged home with home health services for IV antibiotics and follow-up plans with urology and primary care.
problems: Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Epilepsy, unspecified, without mention of intractable epilepsy
Streptococcus infection in conditions classified elsewhere and of unspecified site, streptococcus, group A
Other and unspecified Escherichia coli [E. coli]
Hypertensive chronic kidney disease, unspecified, with chronic kidney disease stage I through stage IV, or unspecified

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ male paraplegic h/o neurogenic bladder s/p ileal conduit w/
longstanding history of bouts of pyelonephritis, left anastamotic
ureteral-conduit stricture treated with PCNU. Patient presents for routine
exchange.

COMPARISON:   Nephro ureteral stent exchange ___

TECHNIQUE:  OPERATORS: Dr. ___ radiology fellow) and Dr.
___ radiology attending) performed the procedure. The
attending, Dr. ___ was present and supervising throughout the procedure.
ANESTHESIA: Moderate sedation was provided by administrating divided doses of
150 mcg of fentanyl and 3 mg of midazolam throughout the total intra-service
time of 30 min during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were
continuously monitored by an independent trained radiology nurse. 1% lidocaine
was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues overlying the access site.
MEDICATIONS: See above
CONTRAST: 30 ml of Optiray contrast.
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE: 1.47 min, 327 cGycm2

PROCEDURE:  1. Left diagnostic nephrostogram.
2. 8 ___  nephrostomy exchange.

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and
alternatives to the procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the
patient. The patient was then brought to the angiography suite and placed
supine on the exam table. A pre-procedure time-out was performed per ___
protocol. The tube site was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.

Diluted contrast was injected into the left catheter to confirm current
position. The image was stored on PACS. Local anesthesia was administered with
instillation of lidocaine jelly and 1% subcutaneous lidocaine injection. The
catheter was cut. A ___ wire was advanced into the catheter and advanced
into the ileostomy. The proximal retaining loop was unformed. The catheter was
removed over the wire.

A new 8 ___ x 22 cm nephroureteral stent was cut at the mid portion of  the
distal pigtail to prevent the catheter from protruding out of the patient's
ileostomy as it was done in the prior procedure. The catheter was advanced
over the wire into appropriate position. The stent was easily advance past the
narrowing at the ureteropelvic junction.  The wire was withdrawn to form a J
loop in the distal catheter. The proximal retention loop was formed and
contrast injection confirmed appropriate positioning. The final image was
saved. The catheter was then flushed. The catheter was secured with 0-silk
suture and a Stat Lock device and sterile dressings. The patient tolerated the
procedure well and there were no immediate post-procedure complications.

FINDINGS: 

1. Left UPJ narrowing.
2. Distal left ureteral stricture at ileostomy anastomosis.
3. Appropriate final position of a left nephroureteral stent.

IMPRESSION: 

Successful exchange of a 8 ___ 22 cm nephroureteral stent on the left,
modified by cutting 2 cm off the tip to prevent pre-catheter from protruding
out of the patient's ileostomy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of your doctors here. You came in last night with nausea and left flank pain. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had this left side pain for a couple days. Then last night I started throwing up. No fever though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your nephrostomy tube was capped when you arrived. We uncapped it, and there was pus draining. That suggests an infection in your left kidney.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh great. Not again. That tube’s always causing trouble.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Your labs show your white count is up, and your kidney function is worse than usual. We’re starting you on meropenem for the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. I hope it works. What about the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re arranging for Interventional Radiology to replace it. It’s routine, but important to clear the blockage and treat the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Just make sure they don’t let it stick out of the ileostomy again like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. The note says they’ll trim the tip to prevent that. We’ll confirm it’s done right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You had the nephrostomy tube exchange this morning. It went well. They found narrowing at the kidney and stricture near the ileostomy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why it was blocked? Is it fixed now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they put in a new stent. It’s draining well. We’ll keep you on antibiotics for about a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my kidney numbers? They were bad last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine was 4.3 on admission. We’ll watch it closely. With treatment, it should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture came back. It grew Stenotrophomonas. That’s why we’re using meropenem—it covers that bug.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? I’ve never heard of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a resistant organism, but meropenem works well. We’ll finish the course and monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing okay, but we noticed your sodium is low—125. Any idea why you might be drinking a lot of fluids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been thirsty. Drink water, juice, Gatorade. Is that a problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With your kidney disease, you can’t get rid of extra water easily. Too much can drop your sodium. We’ll ask you to limit to about 2 liters a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Two liters? That’s not much. But okay, I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sodium is up to 128. Good job on the fluid restriction. We’ll keep watching it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any change in the kidney numbers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Creatinine is down to 3.0. That’s a good sign the infection and blockage are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning a trial to cap your nephrostomy tube tomorrow. If you don’t have pain or swelling, we can discharge soon after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if it doesn’t work? Last time it got blocked again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor closely. If there’s any issue, we’ll unclog or replace it. But the new stent should help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We capped the tube this morning. You’ve had no pain so far—that’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel okay. No pain. But I’m nervous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep checking your kidney function and scan if needed. If all goes well, you could go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry, but your creatinine went up after capping. We had to unclog the tube. It’s now draining again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s blocked again? Why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The stent may have gotten clogged. We’re scheduling another exchange to make sure it’s working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had the second stent exchange today. They confirmed the old one was occluded. The new one is in place and draining well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will this one last longer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s the same type, but we’ll monitor. You’ll need routine changes every three months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture today showed yeast. It’s likely not causing infection, but we’ll watch for symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I need treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. It’s common with catheters. We’ll keep the area clean and monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sodium is now 133—back to normal. Great job limiting fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel thirsty, but I’m sticking to it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. Your kidney function is also improving—creatinine is 2.8.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to try capping the tube again. This time, we’ll watch even more closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hope it works. I just want to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you passed the cap trial. No rise in creatinine, no pain. We’re planning discharge in a couple days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your usual meds. Limit fluids to under 2 liters. Watch for fever, pain, or drainage changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your nephrologist recommended vein mapping for future dialysis access. They’d like to see you in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want that. My kidneys are bad, but I’m not ready for dialysis talks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll note your decision. But it’s important to plan ahead as your CKD progresses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge. You’ll go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve completed the 7-day course. No need for more. Just keep an eye on symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re doing well—no pain, stable labs, tube capped and working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Urology will schedule your next tube exchange in three months. Primary care and nephrology will see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the lung nodule from last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You need a follow-up CT in three months. Your PCP will arrange that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember—fluids under 2 liters, watch for fever or pain, and keep your appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in before discharge. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve added ondansetron for nausea, just in case. Take it as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ll keep it handy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Discharge is set for tomorrow. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think we covered it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call if you have fever, pain, or nausea that won’t go away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check. You’re alert, pain is stable, vitals normal. Discharge is confirmed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ready when you are.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nursing is finalizing your meds and instructions. You’ll get a copy to take home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ll keep it with me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Transport is here. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re officially discharged. Keep up the good work with fluids and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your discharge summary says to limit fluids to less than 2 liters daily. Please stick to that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Water, juice, Gatorade—all under 2 liters.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And call if anything changes. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. We’re here if you need us.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with nausea and left flank pain, found to have a left-sided pyelonephritis due to a malfunctioning nephrostomy tube. He had leukocytosis and acute-on-chronic kidney injury. The tube was draining pus, and urine culture grew Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, treated with a 7-day course of meropenem. He underwent two nephrostomy tube exchanges due to occlusion, with the second allowing successful capping. Hyponatremia developed due to excessive fluid intake and CKD, improving with fluid restriction to less than 2 liters daily. Renal function improved, with creatinine decreasing from 4.3 to 2.8. He passed the capping trial, was discharged home, and advised to follow up with urology, nephrology, and primary care, including a repeat CT for a known lung nodule.
